listenings.text: Every September a family sits in my office and asks me the same question, and I always answer it with a number before anything else. About twenty hours a week, once you count the travel. Eight hours of training, three on match day, four on the bus every second week, and five in study hall. I say it first because families find out anyway, usually in October, and it is better that they hear it from me in a quiet room. Then I tell them the second thing, which is harder to say out loud. Most first-year grades go down. Not all of them, but most. They come back up in the second year, and the students who leave the program almost always leave during that first bad term, before anything has had time to recover. What I refuse to do is argue that sport builds character, because I cannot measure character and neither can you. What I can measure is who finishes. Our athletes complete their degrees at a higher rate than the campus average, and they have done that for eleven years running. That is the argument I make, and it is the only one I need.

People always assume I left the team because I was not good enough, and I understand why, because that is the usual story. It is not what happened. I left because I wanted the engineering degree more than I wanted another season, and by the end of the second year those two things did not fit in the same week any more. Something had to go, and I chose. What surprises people is the next part. I do not regret the first year at all. My English came out of that year, and so did my confidence, because you cannot spend nine months on a bus with fourteen people and stay quiet. If somebody asked me today whether they should do one season, I would say yes without thinking about it. So the argument everybody has, about whether sport is good for students or bad for them, is the wrong argument. The real question is how long you keep doing it. One season is an investment. Four seasons is a career decision, and almost nobody talks about it that way.
